safetyNote: Russula virescens is listed as edible by DGfM and VAPKO, but an illustration or an app can never identify a collected mushroom reliably. Check the entire specimen, especially the base, and do not eat an uncertain mushroom. A brittle russula without a ring or volva cannot be identified as R. virescens on those features alone; the death cap is deadly. Have mushrooms checked by a qualified expert if in doubt.

sections.title: Green mosaic cap
sections.text: The cap is usually 5–12 cm across, occasionally about 15 cm. It starts convex, expands and may become depressed in the centre. Its matt cuticle ranges from pale green to olive or verdigris and splits into small polygonal patches that reveal paler flesh: this is the species’ most recognisable feature. The cap may fade, and its margin may become slightly striate with age.

sections.title: Cream gills and brittle stem
sections.text: The gills are crowded, white to cream and fragile; descriptions place them from adnate to nearly free, and they may develop brown or reddish spots with age. The white, cylindrical stem is about 4–9 cm tall and 1.5–3 cm wide. It is brittle, may brown with age or handling, and can become hollow. Like other brittlegills, this mushroom has no ring or volva.

sections.title: Flesh, spore print and habitat
sections.text: The flesh is white, firm and then brittle, with a faint, sometimes fruity smell and a mild taste. The spore print is white. Russula virescens forms mycorrhizal associations with trees and grows from the soil in broadleaf or mixed woods, especially with oaks, chestnuts and beeches. It fruits in summer and autumn; the observed season varies by region.

traits: Pale green to olive, matt cap, usually 5–12 cm, cracked into polygonal patches over a paler background
Crowded, brittle white to cream gills, sometimes spotted brown or reddish with age
White, cylindrical, brittle stem, about 4–9 × 1.5–3 cm, sometimes browning and becoming hollow
White, firm then brittle flesh with a faint smell and mild taste; white spore print
Mycorrhizal in broadleaf or mixed woods, especially with oaks, chestnuts and beeches · summer and autumn
No ring or volva; their absence alone does not confirm a safe identification
